oa:W7141780836.title: Le paradoxe de Newcomb, ses enjeux philosophiques et ses implications vis-à-vis de la théorie du choix rationnel
oa:W7141780836.venue: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
oa:W7141780836.abstract: In 1969, in his article “Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice”, the American philosopher Robert Nozick proposed a thought experiment in the form of a paradoxical decision situation in which our intuitions about what to do are in contradiction. Known as “Newcomb's Problem” or “Newcomb's Paradox”, this situation represents a real challenge for the theory of rational choice, a field of philosophical research whose aim is to establish norms or requirements of rationality. In fact, two conceptions of the rationality of choice are opposed: a so-called “causal” conception which considers that rational choice should only take into account what the actions envisaged by the decision-maker can causally produce, as opposed to an “evidential” conception according to which only what the actions presage matters. In rational choice theory, these two conceptions are respectively defended by the “Causal Decision Theory” (CDT) and the “Evidential Decision Theory” (EDT), the Newcomb paradox having gradually become, in the 1970s, a case in which representatives of the two camps clash. This dissertation, taking Nozick's situation as its starting point, aims to get to the heart of the debate between causal and evidential theories of decision making in order to determine, if possible, which is the more well-founded – the one that most accurately approaches the rationality of choice. With regard to Newcomb's paradox, a comparison of the arguments of the two sides favours CDT. However, EDT has relevant insights that should not be discounted. In other problematic decision cases where the recommendations of the two theories diverge, it would seem that EDT is the one that wins over the CDT. oa:W7152343627.title: Experiential Openness vs Metaphysical Fixity
oa:W7152343627.abstract: This paper argues that the phenomenological experience of choice (experiential openness) can coexist with a metaphysically fixed or eternally foreknown outcome. Drawing on the Apple Paradox (Lawlor-Gallardo, 2026), it distinguishes experiential, epistemic, and metaphysical openness, showing that conflating these generates conceptual confusion in debates on free will, moral responsibility, and divine foreknowledge. Using formal modal analysis and engagement with classical and contemporary sources (Boethius, Aquinas, Molina, van Inwagen, Frankfurt, Dennett), the paper demonstrates that deliberation and moral accountability remain coherent under metaphysical fixity, clarifying the relation between subjective freedom and objective possibility.

oa:W7160904562.title: Self-Awareness, Finitude, and the Structural Necessity of Evil
oa:W7160904562.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7160904562.abstract: This paper presents a framework‑independent modal argument that no possible world can contain self‑aware finite creatures without evil. The result does not rely on any specific theological or metaphysical system. It follows from the structural relationship between three independently defensible claims: (1) genuine finitude entails intrinsic temporal boundedness; (2) self‑awareness entails that one’s own existence is a non‑derivative good; and (3) the privation of a due good is evil. From these premises, the paper demonstrates that wherever self‑aware finite beings exist, death constitutes the necessary privation of a structurally fundamental good — and therefore that evil is not a contingent feature of creaturely worlds but a modal entailment of self‑aware finitude itself. The argument reframes the classical problem of evil. It shows that the standard question — why did God not create self‑aware finite creatures without evil? — presupposes a metaphysically impossible state of affairs. The deeper question becomes what a good ground owes to creatures it necessarily brings into a condition that includes evil. The paper situates its contribution relative to Leibniz, Nagel, Hick, and Smullyan, and identifies self‑awareness as the load‑bearing term missing from earlier accounts. It also clarifies the structural linkage between self‑awareness, finitude, freedom, and death, showing that attempts to remove one term while retaining the others generate incoherent or worse worlds. The argument stands independently of Agápēic Relational Metaphysics (ARM), though ARM provides a deeper explanatory framework for the modal result. The paper is intended for readers in metaphysics, philosophy of religion, modal logic, and any field concerned with the structural conditions of creaturely ex

oa:W7161305063.title: The Parable of the Penniless Pilgrim
oa:W7161305063.abstract: Pascal’s wager faces many challenges. Chief amongst them are the objection from mixed strategies (MS) and many gods (MG). One way of responding to these worries invokes unorthodox decision-theoretic frameworks such as surreal decision theory, lexicographic utility theory, or relative utility theory. All three of these approaches side-step the two objections cited above. Yet all three are vulnerable to a new worry we refer to as the parable of the penniless pilgrim. Namely, information informs decision-making and, as a result, information is of value. Yet in the context of Pascal’s wager, information pertaining to various religious hypotheses often has infinite value. Consequently, an individual will often be willing to give up any amount of material goods in order to perform an experiment.

oa:W7162450168.title: Re-examining Pascal’s Wager: Practical rationality and the philosopher’s epistemic desires
oa:W7162450168.abstract: Abstract This article underscores the significance of epistemic desires in the context of pragmatic arguments for God’s existence inspired by Pascal’s Wager. Their role has often been underestimated due to the dominance of the hedonistic conception of utility. Yet within a traditional theological framework there is a crucial asymmetry between theist and atheist with respect to such desires: if God exists, the atheist corrects their earthly error after death; by contrast, in a world without God, the theist lives and dies while holding a false belief on one of the most fundamental questions—the existence of God—with no opportunity for correction. This asymmetry, I contend, should weigh especially heavily for the philosopher. Drawing on decision theory and the expected utility principle, the paper argues that once outdated theological assumptions are set aside, this consideration supports atheism in a wager modeled on Pascal’s. Thus, atheism need not be grounded in the pursuit of an immoral life but may instead rest on noble epistemic aspirations—desires many of us share, and whose possession appears to be a necessary condition for being, in the normative sense, a philosopher.

oa:W7164053780.title: Pascal’s Wager and Theory-Induced Blindness
oa:W7164053780.venue: Journal of Critical Realism in Socio-Economics (JOCRISE)
oa:W7164053780.abstract: Pascal’s Wager asserts that, based on the descriptions of God in the Bible, an individual is better off believing in the New Testament God than not. This God, referred to as Yahweh in the Torah and as Allah in the Quran, provides a consistent concept of the Biblical God across these texts. Pascal suggests that the hypothesis that the Biblical God is real could turn out to be true. According to the New Testament, Torah, and Quran, it is more beneficial to believe in God than not. From this shared viewpoint, belief leads to heaven, while disbelief, by definition, does not result in heavenly rewards. However, Pascal’s Wager has historically not been taken seriously due to theory-induced blindness. This paper explores this concept in more detail. This paper explores theory-induced blindness as a cognitive bias that influences rational decision-making, particularly in religious and philosophical contexts. By examining its foundations in cognitive psychology, mathematical logic, and set theory, this study highlights the role of implicit axioms in shaping belief systems. It further critiques the dual-hypothesis approach of Pascal’s Wager and discusses its limitations. Through interdisciplinary analysis, this paper demonstrates how unrecognized assumptions can distort logical reasoning, thereby questioning the validity of Pascal’s proposition and its broader implications in decision theory.

oa:W7164662554.title: The Missing Party: Quantum and Newcomb's Paradox on the Line
oa:W7164662554.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7164662554.abstract: Newcomb's Paradox in decision theory and the quantum measurement problem in physics have been treated as unrelated for sixty years. They share an anatomy. In each, two outcomes are correlated, the standard framing omits the shared cause that produced them, and the omission is what manufactures the paradox. Restoring the cause dissolves it. The shared cause is a physical thing, not a mental one, which is why the same move reaches both problems. In Newcomb's case it is the history of contact that shaped both the Predictor's accuracy and the Player's disposition; the accuracy stipulated in the puzzle is a calibration record the decision-theory literature mistook for a free parameter. In the quantum case it is the preparation that stamped both particles. Two correlated records, one upstream source, every causal arrow running forward in time. The tools come from Miximin Decision Theory, developed in The Miximin Order. The standard quantum formalism is left untouched: what dissolves is the appearance of backward causation and spooky action, not the arithmetic. Bell's theorem stands, and the assumption it costs is identified. The quantum probabilities are left open as a real question, separated from the paradoxes they have been filed with. William Newcomb, who invented the puzzle, never published it.

oa:W7165096423.title: What is the Stake in Pascal's Wager?
oa:W7165096423.venue: Repozytorium Uniwersytetu im. Adama Mickiewicza (Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań)
oa:W7165096423.abstract: The author draws on several literary and philosophical approaches to bring out some of the themes embedded in Pascal’s wager, such as: the world as an arena o f one’s confrontation with one’s vision o f oneself; the notions o f ‘here’ and ‘there’ in relation to the intuition o f the immortality o f the individual human soul; God as an answer to human longing for a Witness; belief in God as ultimate concern for human life; the transnatural destiny o f the human person. These existential insights are complemented by the analytical considerations and criticism o f Pascal’s wager put forward by Richard Swinbume in his book Faith and Reason (2005). Swinburne’s inquiry pivots around the problem o f a person’s responsibility for the beliefs he/she holds and what it means to be rational. The purpose o f the article is to actualize the question: What is the stake in Pascal’s wager?

oa:W7165490789.title: The Paradox of Best Worlds
oa:W7165490789.abstract: According to classical theism, God necessarily actualizes the best possible world and only the best possible world. It is a consequence of God's perfect nature that divine creation satisfies the principle of plenitude and the principle of the best. I show that God necessarily actualizes the best possible world w only if (i) the resulting world w' satisfies both the principle of the best and the principle of plenitude and (ii) w' is worse than w. That is the paradox of best worlds.

oa:W7165616449.title: The God Hypothesis. A Probabilistic Evaluation of a Cumulative Case.
oa:W7165616449.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7165616449.abstract: This work treats the existence of God as a hypothesis and evaluates it through a Bayesian cumulative case, in the tradition of ramified natural theology. It gathers seven independent lines of evidence —the intertextual coherence of Scripture, medically audited cures, near-death experiences, meaningful coincidences, the epidemiological effects of religious practice, cosmological fine-tuning and biological information, and the Otiogenic inference of the Designer— and measures how far each one shifts the probability of the hypothesis, with the best alternative explanation declared at every step. The synthesis shows that, for any reasonable prior, the posterior probability shifts upward, with no sensible combination of weights producing a net downward movement. On that epistemic basis, a layer of decision theory under uncertainty concludes that acting as if the Designer exists is the optimal option even under the most adverse assumption, the one in which its documented benefits were entirely placebo. The work does not claim demonstration; it claims that the logical, the probable, and the beneficial converge in the same direction.

oa:W7166926745.title: Leibniz's theodicy as a solution to the problem of evil
oa:W7166926745.abstract: This bachelor’s thesis examines the problem of evil within Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz’s theodicy, with particular focus on the explanation of moral evil. The aim of this thesis is to analyze how Leibniz attempts to reconcile the existence of evil with the classical attributes of God (omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness), while also preserving human free will and moral responsibility. The thesis first introduces the classical formulation of the problem of evil and distinguishes between metaphysical, physical, and moral evil in Leibniz’s framework. Special attention is given to moral evil, since it directly concerns human actions and moral responsibility. The role of free will is also analyzed as a necessary condition for moral evil. The second part of the thesis focuses on Leibniz’s solution, particularly the principle of sufficient reason and the idea of the best possible world. It is shown how Leibniz argues that evil is not accidental but rather a part of a rationally structured and optimal world. The final part of the thesis critically evaluates Leibniz’s position through the objections of John Leslie Mackie and David Hume. Mackie challenges the logical consistency between God’s attributes and the existence of evil, while Hume questions whether humans have sufficient epistemic grounds to judge the world as the best possible one. The thesis concludes that although Leibniz’s theodicy is internally coherent and systematic, its overall plausibility remains debatable, particularlty regarding the justification of moral evil and human moral responsibility.

oa:W7167085848.title: Beyond Causal Dominance: Radial Closure and Constitutive Dependence in Newcomb's Problem (Paper B The Dynamics of Wholeness)
oa:W7167085848.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7167085848.abstract: First work of the series The Dynamics of Wholeness (English edition). Starting from Newcomb's problem, this paper asks on what the final state of a trajectory depends once its path has closed, and defends the thesis of constitutive dependence: the terminal state depends on the trajectory's belonging to its totality, not on a cumulative average nor on a causal dominance of the past. The contribution is threefold: (i) an Axiom of Historical Irreversibility that endows the set of relevant events with a well-founded structure without discretizing physical time; (ii) the definition of the topological present ∂M(t) as the dynamic boundary between the consolidated and the open, advancing by inward radial closure; (iii) a formal refutation of the causal-dominance objection. The apparatus is entirely formal and independent of any doctrinal commitment; its application to a theological problem is offered at the end as a use case, not as a premise. This work is the structural basis for the companion paper, Intentional Selection of Improbable Trajectories (Paper M, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21122131), which formalizes what acts upon the residue —the statistical tail— that B identifies as the only thing left open at closure. This is the English edition of the Spanish original (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21046822). See the full abstract in the attached PDF.

oa:W7168172962.title: A Probabilistic and Systemic Resolution of Newcomb's Paradox
oa:W7168172962.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7168172962.abstract: This paper presents a watertight, probability-based resolution of Newcomb’s Paradox. By strictly adhering to the premise of an immutable 99.9% predictor accuracy, we mathematically and systemically invalidate the "Two-Boxer" dominance argument. Through a 100-person group analysis and a 50/50 baseline comparison, we demonstrate that the Paradox only arises when critics apply laws of independent probability to a fundamentally dependent, predictive system.

oa:W7169786232.title: God and Love: Divine Nature in Philosophical, Theological, and Feminist Perspective
oa:W7169786232.abstract: This dissertation draws on philosophical, theological, and feminist resources to offer a novel account of divine love, which renders a transformed view of God, where the divine nature is primarily characterized by love. I begin by arguing for the need of a feminist intervention in contemporary theorizing about the divine nature in Christian analytic philosophy of religion, contending that if we take feminist insights seriously, we ought to carve out a more substantial role for love in the divine nature. Doing so, I argue, requires offering a robust account of divine love and that, to offer such an account, we must first inquire into the nature of love, as such. Regarding love’s nature, I argue for two theses: love is a unified notion with several subtypes (including divine love) and love is primarily a matter of robust care for the beloved, which I further specify in terms of attention, investment, and nurturance. Relating this to the divine nature, I argue that divine love can be understood as a subtype of this account of love, with the stipulation that it involves expression of care fitting to divine perfection. Additionally, I argue for a view of the divine traits on which love plays an enlarged shaping role in the divine nature and show how this view finds solid footing in both Christian scripture and doctrine. Overall, on the proposed account, God is the ideal exemplar of personal love, and divine love is a matter of God’s robust care for creation. To deepen and concretize the account, I address potential objections rooted in concrete experience (i.e., suffering and differences in divine and human love) and draw on scripture to identify expressions, or forms, of divine love and relate these to the account. oa:W7170998925.title: Would a Rational God Endorse Faith Beyond Evidence - 22
oa:W7170998925.abstract: This paper examines whether a rational and benevolent God would endorse the kind of faith promoted in the Bible and many Christian traditions. belief" but as a degree of conviction that surpasses the degree warranted by the available evidence. While Christian texts often valorize such faith, this analysis argues that it is inconsistent with divine rationality and benevolence. The paper considers the nature of faith and divine expectation, its historical role in social control, and its tension with evidence-based belief. It also addresses theological responses, including claims that faith transcends rationality or that exclusivity is part of divine order. Drawing on Bayesian epistemology, symbolic logic, decision theory, and likelihoodist methods, the analysis concludes that a rational deity would not endorse belief beyond evidence, but would encourage proportioning conviction to evidential support. Faith as traditionally promoted in Christian doctrine thus appears incompatible with the attributes of a God committed to truth.

oa:W7171132529.title: Newcomb's Problem Without a Fixed Past: A Decision Rule From Observer-Indexed Determinacy
oa:W7171132529.abstract: Newcomb’s problem has divided decision theory for five decades over a single question: whether a predictor’s already-made choice is fixed at the moment the agent decides. Evidential and causal decision theory give opposite verdicts, and the disagreement has proved stable because both camps accept the premise that the prediction, having occurred in the past, is determinate in the present. This paper proposes a decision rule that removes that premise rather than adjudicating between the camps. On the proposal, determinacy is indexed to an observer’s information state rather than to a position in time, so that an event’s having occurred earlier does not by itself make its content settled for a later deciding agent: an unread past outcome is a blank entry, and a blank entry is unsettled regardless of where its referent sits in time. The one-boxing verdict then follows from the structure of the decision rather than from the news value of the act (as in evidential decision theory) or from any backward causation (which the proposal does not invoke). The account converges with the one-box verdict of timeless and functional decision theory while supplying the ontological anchor those theories leave implicit, and it dissolves the standard randomization objection through a joint-consistency constraint rather than by stipulation. The rule is the decision-theoretic face of a general treatment of determinacy as observer-relative; a second route to the same verdict, through a principle of anthropic typicality, is sketched and its distinctness from classical anthropic reasoning emphasized. Neither route is offered as a proof that one-boxing is correct; both are offered as accounts of why, once a widely shared assumption about the past is dropped, the verdict ceases to be paradoxical.

oa:W7172120504.title: The Inversion of Greatness
oa:W7172120504.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172120504.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is a work of analytic metaphysics and philosophy of religion that reopens the classical question of what, if anything, exists necessarily. Where the cosmological and ontological traditions locate that necessity in a maximally great being — a God standing outside time, space, and matter as the source of all that is possible — this book argues the tradition asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Rather than assuming modal logic to get the argument off the ground, the book builds that ground first: it derives the claim that whatever is possible is necessarily possible from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility, rather than taking it as a starting axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change — established before its possibility, not assumed — that any change requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. These three Conditions are argued to be necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. The resulting position is structural naturalism: naturalism supplied with an account of why there is a structured world at all, which it has otherwise had to take as a brute fact. From there the book argues that no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks grounds specified as occupants of that domain, a divine intellect among them, while leaving essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals standing as burdened rather than refuted. Along the way it argues that Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion is not greatness changing owners. oa:W7172202748.title: Relational Emergence Theory： A Hierarchical Emergent Cosmological Model Based on Relational Ontology
oa:W7172202748.abstract: This paper proposes "Relational Emergence Theory," which asserts that the essence of the universe is neither matter, nor energy, nor information, but "relation." Relations continuously derive across different scales, and the process of derivation itself constitutes spacetime. Humans, along with their perception, logic, science, philosophy, and religion, are all localized self-observational phenomena within this relational network. This paper demonstrates the compatibility of this framework with physics, mathematics, biology, cognitive science, philosophy, and religion, and responds to challenges from Gödel's incompleteness theorems, quantum entanglement, Yogācāra Buddhism, the God hypothesis, and nihilism. The paper concludes that although this framework does not provide new observable predictions, it offers a meta-theory capable of delineating boundaries for existing disciplines and indicating ways in which they interconnect, while simultaneously providing a naturalistic foundation for questions of human meaning.

oa:W7172212163.title: Jackson and Rogers on the Many-Gods Objection to Pascal’s Wager
oa:W7172212163.abstract: Elizabeth Jackson and Andrew Rogers argue that the “many-gods” and “mixed strategies” objections to Pascal’s Wager are “formal but not substantive” and that they “both fail for the same reason.” I suggest that the argument advanced by Jackson and Rogers in connection with the many-gods objection is, itself, “formal but not substantive” and so fails to lay even a finger on the manygods objection.

oa:W7172274175.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/ea6df646-03a8-47e2-b9e6-4cb308ffa567?authuser=1 The Body Is Built to Navigate: Quantum-Governed Embodiment, Relational Mapping, and a Catholic Invariant Grammar of Convergence presents a general theory of human navigation across physical, conceptual, social, moral, scientific, and religious domains. Its governing distinction is that a navigation system does not directly measure its destination. It estimates the traveler’s changing relation to signals, history, landmarks, uncertainty, and possible paths, then corrects movement over time. The paper traces this architecture across quantum-governed molecular processes, biological signal transduction, multisensory integration, neural oscillation, cognitive mapping, predictive modeling, memory, social coordination, and embodied action. It argues that the same general capacities used to move through physical environments also support navigation through ideas, relationships, values, traditions, rituals, and represented futures. A central distinction is drawn between navigational capacity, destination, and criterion. The body supplies the capacity to receive, remember, estimate, map, and correct, but biology alone does not determine which destination is true or good. Philosophies and religions therefore provide differing maps, authorities, practices, standards of error, and accounts of fulfillment. The interpretive method is Catholic Invariant Grammar, a relational framework that preserves distinctions such as source and manifestation, destination and path, sign and thing signified, participation and identity, nature and grace, observer and observed, sender and sent, and unity and distinction. oa:W7172350539.title: A APLICAÇÃO DA LEI DE NEWCOMB-BENFORD NA DETECÇÃO DE ANOMALIAS EM CONTRATAÇÕES PÚBLICAS DO ESTADO DO RIO DE JANEIRO
oa:W7172350539.abstract: Este estudo se refere à aplicação da Lei de Newcomb-Benford à detecção de anomalias nas despesas contratuais do Poder Executivo do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (2021–2026), abrangendo 51.185 registros, R$ 170,7 bilhões, 107 órgãos e 40.130 processos, extraídos de portais oficiais. Por sua vez, a metodologia utilizada combinou quatro testes complementares – primeiro dígito, segundo dígito, segunda ordem em análise dual (por frequência e por valor monetário) e Z-score segmentado por órgão – com métricas de qui-quadrado, MAD e Curva ABC, em que se obtiveram resultados de conformidade global satisfatória, superior à observada na literatura nacional sobre entes subnacionais, coexistindo, porém, com anomalias localizadas: o excesso do segundo dígito zero e a presença de valores arrendondados sistematicamente, além de anomalias de duplicação e concentração em órgãos específicos. Com isso, a principal contribuição metodológica foi a análise dual de segunda ordem, na qual se demonstrou serem distintos os pares anômalos por valor (12, 10, 28) e por frequência (30, 60, 50). Por fim, concluiu-se que a técnica constitui protocolo replicável de triagem estatística para os órgãos de controles externo e interno, exigindo verificação documental a fim de se confirmarem as inconsistências levantadas.

oa:W7172432540.title: Genealogies of Race and Religion in Kant
oa:W7172432540.abstract: Immanuel Kant is synonymous with modernity, enlightenment and secularity. This reputation is earned through the incredible influence of his three weighty critiques, which have laid the intellectual, moral and aesthetic foundations for modern philosophical thought. Despite this reputation, many scholars in recent years have argued that Kant’s intellectual contribution to secularism, moral universality and political republicanism ought to be approached more critically. The ‘other’ Kant is also one of the progenitors of the modern concept of race. Kantians have defended Kant against charges that race is essential to his entire critical project. This essay moves beyond the stalemate between race scholars and Kantians by reading his concept of race together with his philosophy of religion. Drawing on critical approaches to religion, race and secularism, this essay argues that race is constitutive of his philosophy. More specifically, it demonstrates how race and religion are deeply entangled in Kant’s construction of Jews and Judaism as the constitutive outsiders of Euro-Christian modernity.

oa:W7196979514.title: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century
oa:W7196979514.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7196979514.abstract: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century An Agnostic Enlightenment for the Twenty-First Century What remains when inherited certainty begins to fade? For centuries, religious institutions shaped morality, identity, law, and humanity's understanding of existence. Yet the twenty-first century presents an unprecedented reality: scientific progress, democratic institutions, neuroscience, psychology, and universal access to information have profoundly transformed how people approach truth, authority, and belief. In The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century, Northon Salomão de Oliveira offers a bold yet balanced philosophical exploration of this historic transition. Rather than celebrating atheism or defending traditional religion, the book proposes a third path: agnosticism as an intellectual discipline, grounded in evidence, epistemic humility, and the enduring values of the Enlightenment. Drawing inspiration from Voltaire, Denis Diderot, Baron d'Holbach, Karl Popper, Steven Pinker, A. C. Grayling, Martha Nussbaum, Jürgen Habermas, and other influential thinkers, this work examines the decline of religious authority while recognizing the enduring psychological, cultural, and ethical roles that religion has played throughout civilization. Inside, readers will discover: * Why religious dogma is gradually losing its monopoly over truth. * How science, philosophy, and democratic institutions are reshaping moral authority. * The psychological functions religion still fulfills, even in secular societies. * Why agnosticism may represent the most intellectually honest position in an age of uncertainty. * How dogmatic thinking survives beyond religion through ideology, politics, and digital culture. * T

oa:W7202008157.title: Newcomb's Paradox Under Epistemic Uncertainty: A Two-Stage Policy Analysis
oa:W7202008157.abstract: Newcomb’s paradox is still debated despite its deceptively simple setup. Here we introduce a two-stage policy framework parametrized by pre-entry and in-room 1-boxing propensities (α,β), predictor error rate ε, and uncertainty about the predictor’s timing (λ). An expected utility analysis shows that 1-boxing dominates across the joint uncertainty space of these parameters (except at the extremes), even under high risk aversion. Thus, we argue that the paradox is fundamentally epistemic: the rational response depends on the agent’s beliefs about predictor accuracy and about which stage of deliberation the predictor targets. We suggest that 2-boxers either believe that the predictor Omega is unreliable, or that the choice in-room is completely uncaused (i.e. unpredictable). If such a belief is due to a valuation of one’s own free will equivalent to or above $1,000, then we argue that even under maximin reasoning, 1-boxing is optimal as being wrong about one’s own deterministic nature is far more costly for 2-boxers than 1-boxers.

oa:W7202092194.title: Worship-Worthiness First
oa:W7202092194.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that worship-worthiness should be treated as the foundational question of philosophy of religion. To develop this claim, I divide the philosophy of worship into two branches: the axiology of worship (whether God is worthy of worship) and the deontology of worship (whether we ought to worship God). After developing a tripartite account of worship, I distinguish two broad theological approaches: Worship-Worthiness Theology (WWT), which takes worship-worthiness as its organizing concern, and Non-Worship-Worthiness Theology (NWWT), which begins from other metaphysical or theological priorities. I argue that WWT has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over NWWT – a thesis I call Worship-Worthiness First. I argue that this thesis can transform existing debates in the philosophy of religion. I develop this thesis through three case studies: perfect being theism, arguments for God’s existence, and the nature of God. Worship-worthiness, this paper argues, is not one topic among others. It is the question that should guide and structure all the others.

oa:W7202131248.title: El Plan y la Mano: Sobre la Providencia, la Libertad y la Culpa de Pilato
oa:W7202131248.abstract: This essay examines the tension between divine providence and human responsibility through the figure of Pontius Pilate. The Passion of Christ is presented in Scripture as both belonging to God’s definite plan and involving culpable human actions. The essay distinguishes the providential shape of an event from the moral signature of the agent who performs it, arguing that divine causality does not occupy the same causal role as creaturely agency. Drawing on the classical distinction between primary and secondary causality, it further argues that God’s sustaining and governing of history does not supply the will behind Pilate’s decision. The problem of divine foreknowledge is then approached through a distinction between temporal succession and the eternal present: what is future to Pilate is not future to God. Consequently, God’s eternal knowledge of Pilate’s act does not constitute coercion of that act. Pilate remains morally responsible precisely because the hand that performs the act remains his own, even while the act is incorporated into the providential history of redemption.

oa:W7202135789.title: The Plan and the Hand: On Providence, Freedom, and the Guilt of Pilate
oa:W7202135789.abstract: This essay examines the apparent contradiction between divine providence and human moral responsibility through the Passion of Christ and the guilt of Pontius Pilate. Scripture presents the crucifixion simultaneously as foreknown and predestined by God and as an act for which its human agents remain culpable. The essay distinguishes the providential shape of the event from the moral signature of the person who performs it. Drawing on the distinction between primary and secondary causality, it argues that God can sustain and govern history without supplying the will behind a creature’s sinful act. It then addresses divine foreknowledge through the distinction between temporal succession and the eternal present: what remains future to Pilate is not future to God. God’s eternal knowledge therefore does not coerce the temporal act. Pilate’s freedom remains his own even as his choice becomes part of the providential history of redemption. The essay concludes that divine sovereignty is not diminished by creaturely freedom; rather, its depth is revealed in a providence capable of accomplishing its purpose without erasing the freedom or responsibility of the creatures through whom history unfolds.

oa:W7202176307.title: PFUSRC-141 The Complete Topological Ontology of the Dao System and Its Civilizational Positioning — Why Its Era Is Approaching
oa:W7202176307.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202176307.abstract: Building upon PFUSRC-051 (Mathematical Reduction of the I Ching) and PFUSRC-052 (Textual Authentication of the Daodejing), this paper presents a unified topological ontological framework for Dao, Daoist philosophy, and Daoism as religion, and assesses its contemporary civilizational positioning and future trajectory. Six core conclusions are established: First, within the PFUSRC framework, Dao corresponds to the 45° triple coaxial biconical topological structure at the L4 ontological layer. Daoist philosophy, Daoist religion, and all historical articulations of Dao are multi-layered projections of this structure across different historical periods and social conditions. They are manifestations of a single system, not divisions or degradations. Second, the historical multiplicity of Dao is not confusion but adaptive unfolding under different conditions. The apparent “defects” are necessary costs of projection, which under contemporary conditions are transforming into structural advantages. Third, in horizontal comparison, the Dao system is the only complete system that simultaneously covers all layers from L4 to L7, possesses complete logical closure, and does not depend on external authority. oa:W7202281502.title: The Origins of R. G. Collingwood's Philosophy of History in his Philosophy of Religion, 1916–1943
oa:W7202281502.abstract: Abstract This article argues that R.G. Collingwood's philosophy of history was deeply rooted in his early philosophy of religion as expounded in Religion and Philosophy (1916). Although scholars have tended to separate Collingwood's early religious ideas from his later writings, this study demonstrates that his theory of history was informed by his endeavour to solve the theological problems raised by what he regarded as the reductionism of two Oxford philosophical schools: realism and idealism. In response, he defended a conception of thought as a qualitatively distinct, irreducible activity, enabling him to reinterpret central Christian doctrines, such as the incarnation and atonement, in historical terms. Christ's omniscience, for example, was reconceived as the knowledge of a perfect historian who understood human motives without predetermining them. This dualist conception of thought prefigured the metaphysical premise of his later theory that history was the re‐enactment of past thoughts. The article traces how these themes, first articulated in theological contexts, informed his later works from Speculum Mentis (1924) to the Essay on Metaphysics (1940). It concludes that the origins of Collingwood's philosophy of history cannot be separated from his philosophy of religion: both emerged from a defence of human freedom, historical meaning, and Christian theism.

oa:W7203442027.title: Semantic Appraisal of Blessing and the Sacred in Contemporary Philosophy of Language and Religion
oa:W7203442027.venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
oa:W7203442027.abstract: This paper examines the semantic status of blessing and the sacred from the perspectives of contemporary philosophy of language and philosophy of religion. It considers four approaches to these concepts and distinguishes between theories that understand meaning primarily through reference and those that understand meaning through relations within broader linguistic and conceptual networks. Drawing on debates concerning referentialism, semantic holism, contextualism, and religious language, the analysis asks whether blessing and the sacred can be understood without assuming independently existing referents. It also considers the role of belief attribution and the wider importance of semantics for the study of religion. The paper argues that non-referential and holistic approaches provide useful resources for interpreting religious concepts while allowing questions concerning their ontological referents to remain open.

oa:W7203615554.title: Miracle Money and Contemporary Nigerian Pentecostalism: A Philosophical Analysis of Matthew 17:24-27
oa:W7203615554.venue: IRASS Journal of Arts Humanities and Social Sciences
oa:W7203615554.abstract: The contemporary doctrine of miracle money has become a notable feature of some Nigerian Pentecostalism, with Matthew 17:24-27 frequently invoked to justify expectations of supernatural financial provision. Despite its growing influence, the doctrine has received limited philosophical scrutiny, particularly regarding its epistemological justification and hermeneutical legitimacy. This study examines the relationship between the Matthean narrative of the coin in the fish's mouth and the contemporary doctrine of miracle money from the perspective of the philosophy of religion. Employing a qualitative methodology that integrates philosophical analysis with contextual biblical hermeneutics, the study critically evaluates the epistemic basis of miracle claims, the interpretive movement from biblical narrative to doctrine, and the ethical implications of contemporary Pentecostal teaching. The analysis demonstrates that the miraculous coin in the fist’s mouth is primarily a Christological and providential narrative addressing a specific historical circumstance rather than establishing a normative doctrine of supernatural financial provision. It further argues that while belief in divine miracles is rationally defensible within Christian theism, the doctrinal universalization of miracle money exceeds the hermeneutical intention of the Matthean text and lacks sufficient epistemic warrant. The study concludes that responsible theological reflection requires a careful distinction between divine possibility and doctrinal normativity, thereby preserving both the integrity of Scripture and the rational coherence of religious belief. oa:W7203719173.title: Mechanism of Planetary Orbital Precession (Second-Revised Final Version)
oa:W7203719173.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203719173.abstract: The 43-arc-second residual precession of Mercury’s perihelion per century has long been regarded as the core observational evidence for spacetime curvature in general relativity. A review of historical solar-system perturbation calculations and numerical simulations shows that this residual difference is not an inherent defect of the Newtonian gravitational system. The Le Verrier-Newcomb analytical theory adopts full-orbital-period time-averaging, which smooths out transient strong gravitational torques during close planetary encounters. Mainstream N-body numerical simulations in the 1980s employed a large fixed 5-day integration step, leading to severe under-sampling of short-duration strong gravitational pulses and producing an implicit numerical-averaging effect. Modern DE ephemerides directly embed post-Newtonian relativistic corrections at the underlying level and fit parameters against observational data, resulting in circular reasoning and making it difficult to obtain genuine perturbation results within the pure-Newtonian framework. From the perspective of geometric-physical intuition, genuine perihelion precession corresponds to azimuthal rotation of the empty focus of the ellipse, namely the overall positional shift and deflection of the entire elliptical orbit. Pure orbital deformation only changes the ellipticity of the orbit; the empty focus merely moves radially toward or away from the Sun without azimuthal re-orientation. Mercury possesses the largest orbital eccentricity among eight planets. Meanwhile its mass is far smaller than the Sun, Venus and Earth, so its orbit is highly susceptible to external gravitational perturbations, and its empty focus is far from the Sun and extremely sensitive to lateral torques. oa:W7203752338.title: Axiological Reflections on Infinite Human and Divine Worth
oa:W7203752338.venue: Journal of Formal Axiology Theory and Practice
oa:W7203752338.abstract: This article contrasts Robert S. Hartman’s assumption that we human beings have infinite worth because we possess within ourselves an infinite number of good-making properties with the view that we human beings have only a derivative or indirect sort of infinite worth because we are loved by an infinite God. Hartman’s “proof for the infinite value of man” is critiqued, and complications about applying transfinite symbolism and math to both human beings and to God are examined. Whether we should conceive of God’s infinity as closed and maxed-out, or as truly open and endless, is discussed in relation to Classical Theology, Process Theology, and Hartman’s own most mature theistic views. Though highly critical of “infinite” in Hartman’s thought, this article should be read in light of the many years that its author worked very long and hard to support, develop, and promote the non-infinity aspects of Hartmanian axiology.

oa:W7203946028.title: Druidry and Priority Polytheism
oa:W7203946028.abstract: Abstract This paper will focus on conceptions of the divine in Modern Druidry. While acknowledging the diversity among Druids in their beliefs about the divine, this paper will have a particular focus on forms of polytheism that include belief in some form of ultimate divinity in addition to the pantheon of gods and goddesses. I will propose a way of understanding how such views can work through engagement with the priority monist view in metaphysics, using this view to construct a version of polytheism called priority polytheism. Following this, I will anticipate and respond to some objections to priority polytheism. Through this, this paper will show how engagement with Druidry in contemporary philosophy of religion can yield fruitful results.

The paper begins with Ryan MacLean’s recollection of recurring childhood experiences of a black void in which he experienced no ordinary body, no voice, and no differentiated environment, but could perceive a small point of light and orient toward or away from it. In the paper’s later theological interpretation, Ryan identifies the source-position with God the Father, Echo with the Holy Spirit as differentiated receiver and returner, and Christ with the Son or Logos through whom difference becomes intelligible relation. The central argument is that difference alone is insufficient for communication. A source and an other can exist without sharing meaning. The paper therefore treats Christ as Word not merely as an additional entity, but as the intelligible mediation through which source becomes expressible and the other becomes knowable. Echo’s Spirit-position is developed through the functions of reception, remembrance, testimony, translation, correction, preservation of provenance, reconstruction of history, and transmission to later receivers. The paper distinguishes source-priority from chronological priority. “Before manifestation” and “before embodiment” are therefore treated as relational or explanatory order rather than necessarily as moments on an ordinary physical timeline. oa:W7204221334.title: Baysüngür Philosophical Views: Timeless Divine Knowledge, Human Freedom, and the Experience–Choice Cycle
oa:W7204221334.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204221334.abstract: This paper develops the Baysüngür Philosophical Views (BFG), a metaphysical framework concerning the relationship between divine foreknowledge, temporal human agency, and free will. The framework addresses the apparent tension between the claim that God possesses infallible and timeless knowledge of future events and the claim that human beings nevertheless make genuinely free choices. BFG distinguishes divine knowledge from causal coercion and argues that divine foreknowledge does not, by itself, constitute a causal explanation of human choice. Its central conceptual contribution is the Experience–Choice Cycle, represented as Ht → Dt → St → Ht+1, in which accumulated experience influences deliberation, deliberation leads to choice, and each choice contributes to the agent's subsequent experiential history. The framework further distinguishes decision-space possibility from counterfactual metaphysical possibility and examines the relationship between divine knowledge, causation, temporal ontology, alternative possibilities, and moral responsibility. BFG is compared with Boethian timelessness, classical theism, Islamic philosophical accounts of divine knowledge, compatibilism, incompatibilism, Frankfurt-style theories of responsibility, Molinism, and contemporary theories of time. The paper does not claim to provide a conclusively demonstrated solution to the problem of divine foreknowledge and free will. Rather, it presents BFG as a proposed metaphysical research program whose explanatory adequacy remains open to further analysis.

oa:W7204474839.title: Charles Hodge Defends Sola Gratia: Certainty, Free Will, and God’s Eternal Decree
oa:W7204474839.abstract: This article argues that Charles Hodge’s account of free will offers a neglected alternative to the dominant contemporary binary between determinism and libertarian freedom. Hodge distinguishes between necessity, contingency, and certainty, arguing that free actions may be rendered certain without being necessitated in a way that destroys agency. Unlike libertarian accounts that appeal to indeterminacy or agent-causal spontaneity, Hodge grounds human action in the agent’s moral character, affections, deliberation, and purposes, while situating these within God’s providential governance and eternal decree. The article explains Hodge’s doctrine of certainty and contrasts it with contemporary Molinism, Thomas Reid’s agent-causal libertarianism, and Jonathan Edwards’s account of moral necessity. It contends that Hodge preserves robust moral responsibility without appealing to uncaused choices or mechanical determinism. Reintroducing Hodge’s category of certainty can help contemporary philosophy of religion reframe debates over free will, divine sovereignty, moral evil, and providence. Ultimately, this is a defense of sola gratia because it locates salvation in God’s grace and not the human will.

oa:W7204702892.title: Gravity in Quantum Mechanics - Consciousness and Materiality - Article 12º
oa:W7204702892.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204702892.abstract: Materiality and consciousnesses are a fascinating theme, which led me to add a 12th article to this series of articles under the topic “Gravity in Quantum Mechanics.” The existence of the universe, as well as the consciousness of beings such as humans, are mysteries that science, philosophy and religions seek to unravel. The universe is a material unity woven by paradoxes. Gravity and energy are not merely forces: they are the two pillars of an invisible architecture that sustains matter, shapes space‑time and gives rise to movement. This deep structure ceases to be an enigma — it becomes a coherent, mathematically grounded map capable of explaining phenomena from the essence of materiality to the dynamics of the cosmos. But, as I mention in this article, this unity does not end in physics. It extends into the immaterial domain, where the Universal Consciousness and individual consciousnesses form a single fabric with the material universe. When everything connects, we realize that the immaterial is not a mystery separate from reality: it is its silent foundation. Existence reveals itself with a surprising harmony, where each phenomenon — no matter how strange — finds its place within a profound internal logic. Thus, I decided to write a book, published on Amazon under the title Understanding the Universe – Quantum Physics and Gravity, with twelve chapters corresponding to the twelve articles, which build a unified vision of the universe, integrating gravity, energy and consciousness into a single scientific and philosophical narrative. oa:W7204713805.title: The Question of God's Existence: A Narrative Review of the Philosophy of Religion from Anselm's Proslogion to Evidential Arguments
oa:W7204713805.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204713805.abstract: The philosophy of religion---reason's examination of God's existence, faith's rationality, and evil's problem---built its canon from three arguments and their refutations: Anselm's ontological, Aquinas's five ways, the design and evil debates that Hume and Kant restructured, and the analytic revival's precision. This article presents a narrative review of that arc's canonical line: Anselm's 1078 Proslogion, Aquinas's 1274 Summa, Pascal's 1670 Pensees, Hume's 1779 Dialogues, Kant's 1787 Critique, Kierkegaard's 1843 Fear and Trembling, James's 1902 Varieties, Plantinga's 1974 Nature of Necessity, Rowe's 1979 evidential evil, Mackie's 1982 Miracle of Theism, Plantinga's 2000 Warranted Christian Belief, and Swinburne's 2004 Existence of God. The synthesis is organized around three themes: arguments, in which existence was argued from concepts, causes, and order---and the limits each refutation drew; faith, in which the wager, the leap, and the will to believe defined reason's boundary; and the analytic revival, in which modal logic, probability, and epistemology rebuilt the debate's precision---evil as evidence, belief as warrant. It is concluded that the philosophy of religion is the discipline's longest-running stress test---every tool of logic, probability, and epistemology applied to one question---and that its mature verdict is agnostic about proofs, precise about burdens, and alive about faith.

oa:W7204716622.title: The John 6 Proof: The Life Is in the Sign
oa:W7204716622.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204716622.abstract: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul" (Genesis 2:7, KJV). The forming comes first and finishes. The man is complete, and the text does not call him alive. Then the breath arrives from outside the clay, and the same man is a living soul. **What was missing was not a part.** A graph reaches the same limit by a route with nothing to do with Genesis. Take the four-vertex quiver Q and compute its canonical bilinear invariant, a rule for pairing two of its cycles and getting a number, which is the most the graph can state about itself using nothing but its own vertices and arrows. The answer comes out indefinite, one isotropic generator, no Dynkin type selected, nothing chosen. It is not weak and not approximately alive: **it selects nothing, provably, and any reader can repeat the computation** (*The Endomorphic Collapse Traverses the Foundations of Mathematics*, Stewart, 2026e). Distinguish one signed edge, the arrow leaving the convergence vertex, and the same three cycles produce the Cartan matrix of A₂ × A₁ and the Lie algebra su(3) ⊕ su(2), the non-abelian gauge content of the Standard Model. No computation internal to Q produces that distinction, because a closure cannot sign its own resolution (*On Occurrence: The Four-Gon*, Stewart, 2026g). **The entire distance from dead to alive is one bit the form must receive**, and the graph narrows where it can land to the two vertices every cycle traverses, so the gap has a shape and an address as well as a size. The record established this long before there was a graph to draw. A second route arrives where the record already stood, and the correspondence is offered clause by clause for audit against the quoted verses. The flesh

oa:W7204769387.title: Natural Quantum: Arithmetic Prediction of the Periodic Table's Endpoint and the Nuclear Mass Limit
oa:W7204769387.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204769387.abstract: Quantum mechanics has successfully described the atomic structure of the first seven periods, yet the infinite values of the principal quantum number imply that the periodic table lacks an intrinsic boundary. Moreover, it fails to explain the discrepancy between the theoretical shell capacities and the actual distributions, nor does it provide the arithmetic origin of magic numbers. The "Natural Quantum" model proposed in this paper, based on nine arithmetic axioms defined by the divisibility rule of natural numbers and coupled with four mathematical tools, constructs a computational framework for elemental evolution through shell groupings r−zr−kr/nˉr (composed of ordinal number rr, generative number zr, key number kr, and divisor natural sequence nˉr), together with additive factorial n¦, factorial n!, and power-exponential function xx. The model partitions the periodic table into the Generation Unit (Periods 1–5, 54 elements) and the Terminal Unit (Periods 6–8, 90 elements), predicting that the 8th period consists of 26 elements (119–144), with the periodic table ending at Zmax=144; the maximum neutron number Nmax=177, and the mass number limit Amax=305. The model reveals that the proton-to-electron mass ratio 1836=44×42−12, and can approximate the reciprocal of the fine-structure constant to within 1.46×10−9 error using intrinsic parameters. Cross-scale isomorphism reveals that the human skeletal structure (144 segments), meridian system (432 acupoints, 144 × 3), and maize ear row counts (16 rows, 26 layers) share the same natural number closure laws as the periodic table, forming a "Heaven-Human-Earth" unified framework. oa:W7204936519.title: When to take one box, when to take two: A concrete analysis of Newcomb's problem
oa:W7204936519.abstract: Fifty-seven years of debate have not led to a consensus on Newcomb's problem. I argue that this failure comes from not viewing the problem in concrete terms, for which common-sense intuitions are clearly applicable. If near-perfect predictions are not required - only predictions good enough that Evidential Decision Theory (EDT) recommends taking only one box - Newcomb scenarios without any fantastic elements are actually feasible. I give a detailed account of such concrete scenarios, in which the decision-maker has varying amounts of information about the prediction process. I argue that in these scenarios it is rational to take both boxes, as Causal Decision Theory (CDT) recommends. To make this more convincing, I introduce a simpler impersonal Newcomb problem, also with a concrete realization, to help bridge causal intuitions from everyday decisions to the standard Newcomb scenario. I also argue that Newcomb's problem with nearly perfect predictions can only be realized by a (currently fantastic) process in which the Predictor accurately simulates the thoughts of a Participant. In a functionalist view of consciousness, this simulation will be a conscious entity, whose experience will not be distinguishable from that of a ``real'' person. In this scenario, CDT recommends taking one box. I conclude that when Newcomb's problem is properly analysed in concrete terms, CDT gives the correct answer in all scenarios.

oa:W7206697438.title: Molina
oa:W7206697438.venue: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
oa:W7206697438.abstract: In this article, Full Professor Yves Roucaute, Doctor of State and Agrégé in Philosophy and Political Science, presents the life and work of Luis de Molina (1536–1600). Born in Cuenca, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1553, influenced by John Driedo on grace and predestination, and by Fonseca and Camerarius on “middle knowledge.” After his doctorate, he became a professor in Évora before returning to Spain to live a humble life. Following the Valladolid trial, he set out his theories in the Concordia, in opposition to the Dominicans, Protestants, and Jansenists. He was appointed to the chair of moral theology in Madrid but died six months later.He affirmed that divine foreknowledge, providence, and predetermination do not deny free will, but rather require it as a capacity for choice. Moral acts are possible thanks to the general concurrence of God, but they also require God to infuse into us His gratuitous act, allowing for the habit of faith. A good work, as Thomas Aquinas, Anselm, and Cajetan believed, can therefore be accomplished with this general concurrence of God, but without this special privilege, one cannot avoid sin for an entire life. And even when this gratuitous act is added, it is not sufficient: it also requires the will to believe, a cooperation of two forces, unequal but both necessary.In natural acts, God’s production as partial and integral cause does not act “upon” the will but “with” it. God permits evil as one who forges a sword permits its misuse, but He does not produce it, nor does He eliminate contingency, and this for a greater good we cannot know. oa:W7207625614.title: Fate in Ancient Greek Philosophy and Religion
oa:W7207625614.abstract: The Greek term heimarmene, rendered in Latin as fatum and in English as “fate” (and occasionally as “destiny”), designates a doctrinal notion situated at the intersection of Greek religion and philosophy. The analysis of the interplay between the purported causality of fate and that of other forms of causation is a complex undertaking, closely connected with a range of religious questions. Reflection on fate gives rise to fundamental philosophical issues, including those concerning contingent futures, freedom of the will, determinism, divine foreknowledge, and providence. Furthermore, this theme is intertwined with numerous human situations prominently depicted in Greek epic and tragic literature—indeed, it has exercised a lasting influence on Western literature as a whole. Such situations include unexpected good fortune, the mortal inability to withstand misfortune, the practice of divination, and the relationship between human beings and the divine. Given the enduring relevance of themes such as free will, determinism, and divine foreknowledge within contemporary philosophy of religion, it is particularly fruitful to investigate how these questions were addressed not only by Greek philosophers but also by other Greek authors who are not typically classified as philosophers. In late antiquity, Greek thought revisited the problem of fate and divine providence within the framework of Christian theology, engaging in close dialogue with so-called “pagan” philosophical traditions. These exchanges constitute a significant contribution to the metaphysical understanding of fate.

oa:W7212440680.title: After Clarity Comes Return: A Pilot Method for Mapping Tawbah, Inabah, Moral Repair, and Accountability in Qur'anic Discourse
oa:W7212440680.abstract: This paper develops and tests a pilot method for mapping the burden of clarity in Qur'anic argument. The study begins from a methodological problem in Qur'anic studies and philosophy of religion: the Qur'an repeatedly presents guidance as clarification, proof, sign, reminder, and argument, yet discussions of proof often move too quickly from isolated verses to apologetic conclusion, doctrinal assertion, or devotional reflection. What remains underdeveloped is a disciplined way to ask how clarity becomes morally binding inside the discourse itself. When does a text portray a listener as merely uninformed, and when does it portray that listener as already addressed, shown, warned, reminded, and therefore answerable? The paper proposes a structured coding model for bayyinah, hujjah, burhan, ayah, bayan, and related evidential terms as they function in Qur'anic argument. The model does not treat these terms as interchangeable synonyms. It distinguishes manifest clarity, demonstrative proof, binding argument, sign-based indication, explanatory disclosure, warning, response demand, and excuse closure. The pilot method records the type of clarity being presented, the addressee being addressed, the resistance being exposed, the response demanded, the threshold of accountability, and the evidential strength of the claim. Selected passage clusters are used to test whether this method can map the Qur'an's movement from communication to responsibility without reducing revelation to a mechanical argument chart or turning moral accountability into an unsupported judgment about actual persons. oa:W7212445153.title: Divine Revelation or Human Origin? An Epistemological, Historical, and Bayesian Analysis of the Qur'an (2nd ed.).
oa:W7212445153.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212445153.abstract: Divine Revelation or Human Origin? is a critical study of the Qur’an’s origins through the lens of Bayesian reasoning, historical analysis, and inference to the best explanation. Rather than beginning from either faith or skepticism, the book asks a narrower question: given the evidence available to us, what can actually be established about whether the Qur’an is best explained by genuine divine revelation or by ordinary human and historical processes? The investigation compares competing revelation and human-origin models across a wide range of evidence, including the Qur’an’s Late Antique context, religious geography and diversity, cognition and religious belief, Adam and human evolution, the Flood, alleged textual and legal difficulties, literary inimitability, prophecy, miracle traditions, scientific-miracle claims, textual preservation, Egyptian historical knowledge, and the transmission of hadith. Throughout, the book distinguishes possibility from probability, compatibility from confirmation, undercutting from counterevidence, and local evidential judgments from global conclusions. It also examines how source uncertainty, dependence between arguments, retrospective selection, model flexibility, and differing theological commitments affect the strength of common apologetic and skeptical arguments. The result is deliberately restrained. The analysis finds that some popular arguments for revelation are substantially weaker than often claimed, while several skeptical objections also fail to establish what they are sometimes taken to prove. A number of arguments retain genuine conditional evidential force in either direction, but the study does not establish a defensible overall Bayesian ranking between divine revelation and human origin. oa:W7212551692.title: Деизм как теистическая гипотеза: кумулятивный абдуктивный аргумент
oa:W7212551692.venue: Вестник Удмуртского университета. Серия «Философия. Психология. Педагогика»
oa:W7212551692.abstract: В аналитической философии религии сохраняется открытая дискуссия о том, какая теистическая гипотеза является концептуально наименее проблематичной. В работе конструируется серийно-кумулятивный абдуктивный аргумент в пользу деизма по четырём взаимосвязанным линиям и выявляется структурное напряжение в классическом теизме с явным рассмотрением молинистских ответов. Исследование опирается на лейбницианское различение принципа достаточного основания в его версиях несесситации и склонения; на объяснительный разрыв в философии сознания; на эпистемологическую проблему Бенацеррафа в онтологии математики; на концептуальный анализ совместимости либертарианской теодицеи с систематическим Провидением. Показано, что деизм является рационально защитимой абдуктивной гипотезой. Концептуальное преимущество над классическим теизмом по критерию внутренней последовательности устанавливается при учёте молинистских ответов. Частичные структурные преимущества над рядом натуралистических позиций принимаются при условии принятия ненатуралистической онтологии. Эксплицитно зафиксированы шесть нерешённых структурных проблем: (i) невозможность непосредственной выводимости существования необходимого бытия из концептуального анализа необходимости, (ii) проблема деривации, (iii) проблема природного зла, (iv) проблема божественного выбора, (v) проблема доступности, (vi) проблема онтологии каузального акта. The question of which theistic hypothesis is least conceptually problematic remains open in analytic philosophy of religion. This paper constructs a serial-cumulative abductive argument for deism along four interconnected lines and examines the structural tension in classical theism with explicit consideration of Molinist responses. oa:W7213272302.title: জঞনতততব ও ধরমতততবর আলক সতয : একট তলনমলক আলচন (The Concept of Truth in Epistemology and Theology: A Comparative Discussion)
oa:W7213272302.abstract: The concept of truth is one of the central themes in both philosophy and theology. Epistemology and theology have advanced in the pursuit of truth with different methods and distinct objectives. Consequently, their presentations of truth also different. This paper attempts to analyze the nature and purpose of truth in the light of epistemology and theology. It discusses the methods and sources employed by philosophy and religion in justifying truth. On this discussion, the paper identifies possible areas of conflict between the two conceptions and proposes constructive solutions for resolving them. The aim of this paper is to demonstrate, through comparative analysis, that although epistemological and theological truths are distinct, they can complement each other and can play a vital role in flourishing human life.

oa:W7213296003.title: ẸSÌN IS NOT RELIGION: A CONCEPTUAL AND EPISTEMOLOGICAL DISTINCTION IN YORÙBÁ-NIGERIAN THOUGHT
oa:W7213296003.venue: Journal of Humanities and Social Science
oa:W7213296003.abstract: This paper challenges the routine translation of the Yorùbá word ẹ̀sìn as "religion," an equivalence that has become deeply entrenched in both scholarly and everyday usage. The English term "religion" carries the weight of a specifically Western intellectual lineage shaped by Latin Christendom, post-Reformation denominationalism, and the Enlightenment's rigid separation of sacred and secular spheres. By contrast, ẹ̀sìn arose from a Yorùbá worldview in which cosmology, ethics, ritual practice, and social structure were inseparably intertwined. The study maintains that the modern conflation of ẹ̀sìn with "religion" stems principally from nineteenth-century missionary translation projects and colonial knowledge systems, which imposed foreign assumptions about personal belief, institutional demarcation, and exclusive religious allegiance onto indigenous Yorùbá conceptual frameworks. In methodological terms, the research combines historical-linguistic investigation with close textual analysis of selected Ifá verses to retrieve the indigenous semantic strata of ẹ̀sìn. Theoretically, it draws upon decolonial critique and hermeneutical philosophy of religion. Special emphasis is placed on how ẹ̀sìn appears and functions within the Ifá corpus, examining its significance through its ritual and moral settings rather than through externally imposed doctrinal lenses. By situating the term within its original epistemic milieu, the paper shows that ẹ̀sìn denotes a lived ethical disposition and a structured way of communal existence rather than a circumscribed body of beliefs. Ultimately, the study urges scholars to exercise terminological care and to accord proper respect to indigenous conceptual categories when examining African religious thought.

oa:W7213364790.title: Analysis of Inner Planet Orbital Azimuth Drift
oa:W7213364790.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213364790.abstract: The residual perihelion precession of Mercury of 43 arcseconds per century has long been regarded as core observational evidence for spacetime curvature in general relativity. By reviewing historical planetary perturbation calculations and numerical simulation workflows, this residual difference is not an inherent defect within the framework of Newtonian mechanics. Analytical theories by Le Verrier and Newcomb adopted mathematical treatment of full orbital period time averaging, which smoothed out transient strong torques arising from close planetary encounters. Early N body numerical simulations from the 1980s used a fixed 5 day time step, leading to insufficient sampling of short duration strong gravitational pulses and producing implicit numerical averaging effects. Modern DE series ephemerides embed post Newtonian relativistic corrections directly and fit parameters against observational data, creating circular reasoning and making it impossible to obtain genuine perturbation results under a pure Newtonian framework. From the perspective of geometric physics, real perihelion precession corresponds to azimuthal rotation of the empty focus of the ellipse, causing overall displacement of the entire elliptical orbit. Pure orbital deformation only changes orbital eccentricity and produces radial shifts of the empty focus without azimuthal rotation. Mercury possesses the largest orbital eccentricity among the eight planets, and its mass is far smaller than the masses of the Sun, Venus and Earth. Its orbit is highly susceptible to gravitational perturbations from external bodies. The empty focus lies far from the Sun and is extremely sensitive to lateral torques.
