oa:W7213370651.title: Religion and alienation: towards posing of the probleme
oa:W7213370651.abstract: In the philosophy of religion, the theme of alienation is used rather narrowly, mainly in connection with its sociocentric interpretations, as well as in the context of German classical idealism and materialism. In fact, it turns out that the phenomena behind alienation theories are fundamental and quite universal in the history of human thought. One shall not be wondered by the case that philosophy tends to deal with just such things. The article examines concepts of alienation in the religion studies, and issues related to them in the works of Plotinus, Kant, Hegel, Schelling, Feuerbach, Marx, Kierkegaard, Nesmelov, Nietzsche, and Girard. It is demonstrated that the diversity of approaches to the problem is due to the difference in axiomatic assumptions or to what is taken as basic experience. As a review of concepts, the article aims to show the possibilities of a "cartographic" approach in teaching philosophy of religion.

oa:W7213451243.title: Paganism in the philosophical reflection of Edward Herbert
oa:W7213451243.abstract: The aim of the research is to identify the significance of Edward Herbert of Cherbury's work "The Religion of the Gentiles" for the development of the philosophy of religion and religious studies. The article examines the source base, methods, and content of Herbert's book, in which the author took the study of religion beyond confessional boundaries. At the core of Herbert's philosophical study lies an attempt to justify paganism by proving the unity of the essential religious foundations of all confessions of the past and present. The scientific novelty of the study is associated with the fact that Herbert's book "The Religion of the Gentiles" is considered for the first time as a methodological attempt to substantiate a universal religion based on cross-cultural comparison. As a result of the study, it was established that the book "The Religion of the Gentiles", firstly, is one of the extensive encyclopedias of religious traditions of its time; secondly, it continues and develops Herbert's teaching on a single universal religious foundation; thirdly, the issues raised in the book define religion as an object of philosophical reflection; fourthly, Herbert bases his conclusions not only on the use of diverse sources, but also on comparative analysis, which brings his study closer to the scientific standards of comparative religious studies.

oa:W7213559515.title: Christian Philosophy and Christian Apologetics: A Philosophical Examination of Their Relationship and Complementarity
oa:W7213559515.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RELIGIOUS AND CULTURAL PRACTICE
oa:W7213559515.abstract: In an increasingly pluralistic and sceptical global context, Christianity continues to face sustained intellectual challenges that question its truth claims, coherence, and relevance. These challenges arise not only from overt secularism but also from competing religious worldviews and internal misunderstandings regarding the role of reason in faith. Within this climate, Christian apologetics emerges as a disciplined response aimed at offering rational justification for Christian belief, while Christian philosophy provides the conceptual and methodological framework through which such justification becomes intelligible. This paper examines the relationship between Christian philosophy and Christian apologetics, arguing that the two disciplines are neither identical nor autonomous, but fundamentally interdependent. Through conceptual analysis, historical reflection, and philosophical engagement, the study demonstrates that apologetics depends on philosophical reasoning for coherence, while Christian philosophy finds practical expression and relevance through apologetic engagement. Drawing on key thinkers in philosophy of religion and Christian thought, the paper contends that a robust defence of Christian faith requires philosophical depth grounded within a Christological and biblical framework. The paper concludes that separating Christian apologetics from Christian philosophy weakens both disciplines and undermines the intellectual credibility of Christian faith in contemporary discourse.

oa:W7213583757.title: Newcomb's Problem Without a Fixed Past: A Decision Rule From Observer-Indexed Determinacy
oa:W7213583757.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213583757.abstract: Newcomb’s problem has divided decision theory for five decades over a single question: whether a predictor’s already-made choice is fixed at the moment the agent decides. Evidential and causal decision theory give opposite verdicts, and the disagreement has proved stable because both camps accept the premise that the prediction, having occurred in the past, is determinate in the present. This paper proposes a decision rule that removes that premise rather than adjudicating between the camps. On the proposal, determinacy is indexed to an observer’s information state rather than to a position in time, so that an event’s having occurred earlier does not by itself make its content settled for a later deciding agent: an unread past outcome is a blank entry, and a blank entry is unsettled regardless of where its referent sits in time. The one-boxing verdict then follows from the structure of the decision rather than from the news value of the act (as in evidential decision theory) or from any backward causation (which the proposal does not invoke). The account converges with the one-box verdict of timeless and functional decision theory while supplying the ontological anchor those theories leave implicit, and it dissolves the standard randomization objection through a joint-consistency constraint rather than by stipulation. The rule is the decision-theoretic face of a general treatment of determinacy as observer-relative; a second route to the same verdict, through a principle of anthropic typicality, is sketched and its distinctness from classical anthropic reasoning emphasized. Neither route is offered as a proof that one-boxing is correct; both are offered as accounts of why, once a widely shared assumption about the past is dropped, the verdict ceases to be paradoxical.

oa:W7213590432.title: THE NATURE OF TIME: Trialogue of Science Philosophy and Religion Vision of Time
oa:W7213590432.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213590432.abstract: The phenomenon of time remains one of the most foundational, recalcitrant, and under-determined categories of human inquiry. While the natural sciences successfully formalize and measure the operational properties of time, they lack a universally accepted ontological definition of what time is at the bedrock of Being. Across philosophy and the theological traditions, time is conceptualized through an extraordinarily disparate spectrum of categories and doctrines. This doctoral dissertation undertakes a disciplined investigation of that ontological lacuna. Its architecture is organized as a systematic trialogue among Science, Philosophy, and Religion. The core methodological principle is rigorous epistemic demarcation: the continuous distinction between established empirical or textual facts and metaphysical or theological postulates adopted on non-empirical rational grounds. Part I (Science) identifies the precise junctures at which modern theoretical physics — particularly the problem of time in quantum gravity, the cosmological singularity, and the thermodynamics of non-equilibrium systems — reaches the outer boundary of empirical formalisms.Part II (Philosophy) constructs an autonomous metaphysical architecture upon this threshold: a three-tiered taxonomy of temporality (causal TIME-1, cyclical Time-2, and evental/phenomenal time-3). oa:W7213922601.title: Sacralizing Dominion: The Doctrine of Christian Discovery and the Religious Nationalist Imagination
oa:W7213922601.abstract: White Christian nationalism presents itself as restoration—of a Christian nation, a moral order, a rightful hierarchy. This article argues that what it restores is the world-making rhetoric of the Doctrine of Christian Discovery (DoCD). Reading the fifteenth-century papal bulls, their sedimentation into United States law, culture, religion, and contemporary dominionist discourse as a single rhetorical formation, we show that the bulls’ vocabulary of discovery, vacancy, and civilization did not describe a world but constituted one: a moral-legal order in which Christian identity conferred sovereignty and racialized peoples appeared as obstacles to salvation and property. That order persists as hegemonic common sense, carried by legal precedent, curricula, and popular culture, and it is re-performed today in the territorial rhetoric of the New Apostolic Reformation and white Christian nationalism. Following Steven T. Newcomb (Shawnee/Lenape), repudiating the doctrine’s documents without dismantling its embeddedness within language and cognition leaves religious nationalism’s deepest resource intact. Against the discovery template, we set three counter-rhetorics—Indigenous theologies, Black theology, and womanism—and argue that desanctifying dominion requires conciliation, not reconciliation.

oa:W7213957072.title: «ЧЕЛОВЕК МАССЫ» И БУДУЩЕЕ ХРИСТИАНСТВА: РАЗМЫШЛЕНИЯ НАД ФИЛОСОФИЕЙ ИСТОРИИ РОМАНО ГВАРДИНИ
oa:W7213957072.venue: The Quarterly Journal of St Philaret s Institute
oa:W7213957072.abstract: Книга видного католического мыслителя, священника Романо Гвардини «Конец Нового времени» (1950) предлагает такое видение истории, которое позволяет избежать представления как о ее единой направленности, так и о ее анонимности, и тем самым раскрывает и новое христианское понимание истории. Анализируя картину мира Средневековья, а также мировоззренческий переворот Нового времени, Гвардини представляет каждую эпоху и даже самые угрожающие ситуации как некий шанс, дарованный Богом, — как καιρός, благоприятный миг и уникальный дар, открывающий новые возможности, который, однако, может быть и безвозвратно упущен. Именно с этих позиций он анализирует и крушение идеалов Нового времени, и современное ему, пугающее явление «человека массы», знаменующее собой начало новой эпохи. В отличие от других мыслителей — Ортега-и-Гассета и Х. Арендт, также писавших о «человеке массы», однако в сугубо отрицательном ключе — Гвардини пытается увидеть положительный смысл этого явления. Вместо того чтобы сожалеть о безвозвратно ушедшем идеале богатой талантами уникальной личности, следует понять, каковы новые возможности и новая задача, стоящая перед «человеком массы». Гвардини формулирует ее как сохранение «лица» (Person), незаменимого в своем достоинстве и незаместимого в своей ответственности, а также как противостояние безликим анонимным силам, все более овладевающим человечеством. С точки зрения Гвардини, ответственность тут лежит прежде всего на христианах, поскольку именно христианская вера дает обоснование бесконечной ценности каждого человеческого «лица». Сегодня, 75 лет спустя после выхода в свет книги Гвардини, стоит задаться вопросом не только о том, насколько продуктивным оказался его взгляд на историю, но и о том, оправдались ли его надежды на осуществление христианского призвания

oa:W7213970661.title: Religious non-realism: expanding an idea
oa:W7213970661.abstract: Abstract In this study, I seek to rehabilitate the notion of ‘religious non-realism’, which is misunderstood in the philosophy of religion and significantly underdeveloped. I begin by widening the scope of the idea to encompass both propositional and non-propositional phenomena, and then focus on non-realist religious practice, expanding beyond what I call discourse-centred practices – focused on mobilizing substitutes for realist interpretations of religious discourse; expressivism and fictionalism suggest examples – to practices whose non-realism is discourse-independent. Once discourse-independent non-realist practices are acknowledged, a further distinction presents itself. Non-realist religious practice may be governed by a single idea – such as an expressivist or fictionalist idea – or it may integrate multiple such ideas. I call the former sort of non-realism monist and the latter mixed . Taken together, these distinctions reveal a range of structurally distinct forms of non-realist (and thus non-believing) religion, including mixed possibilities that have received no attention in the literature. By bringing the latter into view through concrete examples drawn primarily from Christianity, the study shows that the discussion of non-realist religious practice admits of a richer depiction, and one perhaps also more true to life, than philosophy of religion has so far supplied.

oa:W7214001856.title: From Tripartite Freedom to Fair Opportunity: T. H. Green and David O. Brink
oa:W7214001856.abstract: This article examines the structural relationship between T. H. Green’s tripartite conception of freedom and David O. Brink’s fair opportunity account of moral responsibility, arguing that the traces of Green’s model can be discerned in the conceptual architecture of Brink’s account. Green’s conception emerges from a critical engagement with Kant’s account of freedom and responds to Sidgwick’s objection that Kant cannot adequately explain how wrongdoing can be both free and responsible. By identifying moral freedom with the capacity for reasons-responsiveness rather than with its proper exercise, Green defends the spirit of Kantian freedom while addressing its principal weakness. Green distinguishes three dimensions of freedom: juridical freedom as the absence of external coercion; moral freedom as the capacity for reasons-responsiveness that grounds responsibility; and real or perfect freedom as the virtuous actualization of that capacity in pursuit of self-realization and the common good. These three dimensions are not rivals but complementary conditions for the full realization of moral personality. Green’s account of perfect freedom, with its emphasis on self-realization and the common good, also carries a distinctly religious dimension, addressing questions about human nature, divine justice, and moral accountability that situate his tripartite model within the broader concerns of the philosophy of religion. While Berlin’s critique reads Green’s positive freedom as dangerously close to authoritarian justification, and while Weinstein, Simhony, and Dimova-Cookson offer divergent reconstructions of Green’s account, this article takes as its starting point Brink’s reconstruction of Green’s framework within the Kantian tradition. oa:W7214094597.title: Axiality and Pluralism: Karl Jaspers and the Search for a Global Philosophy of Religion
oa:W7214094597.abstract: Abstract The paper addresses the concepts of globality, universality, and pluralism in contemporary philosophy of religion. We argue that embracing a form of pluralism is essential to meet the growing demand for inclusivity in the philosophical study of religions, although this does not equate with any rejection of the classic Western tradition. To support this argument, we explore Karl Jaspers’ notion of the Axial Age ( Achsenzeit ) and its relevance to this discussion. We begin with a brief overview of the theory, emphasizing the religious elements it encompasses and its implications. The Axial Age is recognized as a period during which both major world religions and diverse spiritual experiences and practices emerged. This significance becomes particularly evident in contemporary discussions by authors such as Jan Assmann and Jürgen Habermas. We therefore propose that the Axial Age could serve as a useful model for the philosophy of religion. However, we also note that it requires substantial modifications. On one hand, the concept is more Eurocentric than it initially appears; on the other hand, it is inherently open to a truly global perspective and can effectively describe various forms of religiosity. As proof of this thesis, we conclude by focusing on the connection between these issues and the themes of secularization and post-secularization.

oa:W7214365228.title: Natural Quantum: Arithmetic Prediction of the Periodic Table's Endpoint and the Nuclear Mass Limit
oa:W7214365228.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214365228.abstract: Quantum mechanics has successfully described the atomic structure of the first seven periods, yet the infinite values of the principal quantum number imply that the periodic table lacks an intrinsic boundary. Moreover, it fails to explain the discrepancy between the theoretical shell capacities and the actual distributions, nor does it provide the arithmetic origin of magic numbers. The "Natural Quantum" model proposed in this paper, based on nine arithmetic axioms defined by the divisibility rule of natural numbers and coupled with four mathematical tools, constructs a computational framework for elemental evolution through shell groupings r−zr−kr/nˉr (composed of ordinal number rr, generative number zr, key number kr, and divisor natural sequence nˉr), together with additive factorial n¦, factorial n!, and power-exponential function xx. The model partitions the periodic table into the Generation Unit (Periods 1–5, 54 elements) and the Terminal Unit (Periods 6–8, 90 elements), predicting that the 8th period consists of 26 elements (119–144), with the periodic table ending at Zmax=144; the maximum neutron number Nmax=177, and the mass number limit Amax=305. The model reveals that the proton-to-electron mass ratio 1836=44×42−12, and can approximate the reciprocal of the fine-structure constant to within 1.46×10−9 error using intrinsic parameters. Cross-scale isomorphism reveals that the human skeletal structure (144 segments), meridian system (432 acupoints, 144 × 3), and maize ear row counts (16 rows, 26 layers) share the same natural number closure laws as the periodic table, forming a "Heaven-Human-Earth" unified framework. oa:W7214424872.title: Review of Timothy Bowers Vasko, Making All the World America: Native Information and the Doctrine of Discovery (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2026)
oa:W7214424872.abstract: Steven T. Newcomb reviews Timothy Bowers Vasko's Making All the World America: Native Information and the Doctrine of Discovery (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2026). Vasko argues that the Doctrine of Discovery worked not through the suppression of Indigenous peoples but through European recognition of Indigenous rights and sovereignty, incorporating Native peoples as religious, political, and property-owning subjects. Newcomb finds this reading inaccurate and incomplete. Applying his "domination translator," he shows that Vasko's key terms—dominium, dominion, sovereignty, empire, incorporation—all resolve into the Christian European claim of a right of domination over non-Christian nations. The review faults Vasko for omitting an etymology of dominium, for passing over the explicit language of domination in the papal bulls of 1452, 1455, and 1493, and for misstating the Vatican's March 2023 statement as a repudiation of those bulls. Newcomb concludes that "discovery" is not the issue; the continuing claim of a right of domination is.

oa:W7214575129.title: The Leading Digit Is 1 Three Times in Ten, but Only for Data Spread Across Many Orders of Magnitude ── Among 2^n for n=1 to 10000 the leading digit is 1 in 0.301000 of cases, within 0.000092 of log_10(1+1/d) for all nine digits ── the dividing line is whether the data spread across orders of magnitude ── [Paper 612]
oa:W7214575129.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214575129.abstract: Counting which of 1 to 9 is the leading digit (the top digit) in a list of numbers often gives about three in ten for 1 and under five per cent for 9 (Benford's law). For which data it holds, and for which it does not, is counted. No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──that leading digits are uneven (Newcomb, 1881; Benford, 1938), that the only distribution unchanged by rescaling is this law (Pinkham, 1961), that numbers drawn from a mixture of distributions approach it (Hill, 1995), and that the fractional parts of nlog_102 spread evenly (Weyl, 1916) are all known. Applications are not treated──detecting fraud in accounts and the like are not entered. Why so much real data follows it is not discussed──data that follow and data that do not are only sorted and counted by how far they spread in orders of magnitude. Relation to earlier papers: Paper 117 separated four ways in which scale invariance fixes an exponent──this paper confirms in numbers that, for leading digits, a distribution unchanged by rescaling is log_10(1+1/d). What is added is counting the leading digits of 10000 powers of 2 exactly as integers, setting side by side that tripling changes nothing while doubling uniform numbers changes the shares, and placing the separator on whether the data spread across orders of magnitude, measuring the spread of uniform numbers, heights and products in orders. oa:W7214661031.title: Prospettive di Storia di Filosofia della Religione. Per un confronto critico tra Alberto Caracciolo e Pietro Piovani
oa:W7214661031.venue: Nuovo Giornale di Filosofia della Religione (NGFR)
oa:W7214661031.abstract: Il saggio propone un confronto critico tra le prospettive filosofiche di Alberto Caracciolo e Pietro Piovani, con particolare rilievo per l’interpretazione che i due autori delineano del Concilio Vaticano II. Il testo si articola in tre sezioni: nella prima imposto in breve la metodologia utilizzata, sottolineando l’opportunità di un’analisi storico-culturale anche per la filosofia della religione; nella seconda istituisco un serrato raffronto tra Caracciolo e Piovani, specie per quanto attiene la pubblicazione de La religione come struttura e modo autonomo della coscienza (1965) e la sua discussione da parte del filosofo napoletano (poi raccolta nel volume dell’anno successivo Conoscenza storica e coscienza morale); l’ultima sezione è invece interamente dedicata all’interpretazione conciliare. Parole chiave: Filosofia della religione, Filosofia della storia, Alberto Caracciolo, Pietro Piovani, Concilio Vaticano II The essay proposes a critical comparison between Alberto Caracciolo and Pietro Piovani, with a particular emphasis on the interpretation that the two authors outline of the Second Vatican Council. The text is divided into three sections: in the first, I briefly set out the methodology used, emphasizing the appropriateness of a historical-cultural analysis of the philosophy of religion; in the second I establish a close comparison between Caracciolo and Piovani, especially concerning the publication of La religione come struttura e modo autonomo della coscienza (1965) and its discussion by the Neapolitan philosopher (later collected in Conoscenza storica e coscienza morale); the last section is instead entirely devoted to the Council’s interpretation. oa:W7214910569.title: Mercy and Justice in the Context of John 8:1-11: A Philosophy of Religion Perspective
oa:W7214910569.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214910569.abstract: This paper offers a philosophical evaluation of the relationship between justice and mercy in the narrative of the adulterous woman in John 8:1-11, addressing the central question of whether mercy constitutes a violation or fulfillment of justice. The study begins by situating the narrative within its legal and moral framework, highlighting the apparent retributive demands of Mosaic Law alongside the procedural and ethical deficiencies in its application. Through a rigorous conceptual analysis, the paper engages classical and contemporary philosophical accounts of justice from Aristotelian equity and Kantian retributivism to Rawlsian fairness and Wolterstorff’s rights-based approach while also examining the moral logic of mercy as articulated in both classical theology and modern ethical theory. The analysis argues that the tension between justice and mercy arises primarily from a reductive understanding of justice as strict retribution. By contrast, a broader philosophical framework incorporating equity, dignity, and restorative aims reveals that mercy need not negate justice but can function as its highest expression. Drawing on restorative justice theory and contemporary critiques of punitive models, the paper interprets Jesus’ response as a form of moral intervention that exposes the limitations of legal formalism and reorients justice toward moral transformation. The refusal to condemn the accused, coupled with the call to ethical renewal, reflects a conception of justice that integrates accountability with the possibility of restoration. Within the framework of philosophy of religion, the paper further argues that this narrative provides a coherent account of divine moral action in which justice and mercy are not contradictory but mutually implicative. oa:W7215108450.title: Beyond Performative Morality Based on A Thematic Interpretation of The Satya-Māyā Dialectic in The Ethics of Power of Śakuni and Kṛṣṇa in The Mahābhārata
oa:W7215108450.abstract: The phenomenon of performative morality and religiosity in the contemporary public sphere (moral and religious expressions intended for public consumption, rather than the manifestation of inner dispositions) highlights the need for a conceptual framework that distinguishes between ethical appearance and substance. This research develops a thematic-hermeneutic reading of the satya-māyā dialectic in the Mahābhārata, examining how Śakuni and Kṛṣṇa represent two opposing ethical orientations within the relationship between truth and power. This study of the philosophy of religion employs a hermeneutic-phenomenological approach to the dice-playing episode in the Sabhā Parva and selected ślokas from the Bhagavad Gītā, combined with a comparative analysis drawing on political realism. The results indicate that Śakuni represents the instrumentalisation of truth and morality as tools of power, whilst Kṛṣṇa articulates an ethic that subordinates power to satya and dharma through niṣkāma karma. Māyā is understood as an epistemological condition that enables the disjunction between appearance and essence, whilst sattva and lokasaṅgraha form the textual basis for leadership with integrity. Performative morality and religiosity are formulated as new analytical categories that bridge performativity theory with the conceptual structure of the Bhagavad Gītā, characterised by the gap between appearance and essence, the instrumentalisation of symbols, and visibility, accompanied by critical scrutiny of Kṛṣṇa’s controversial actions, without theological justification. oa:W7215115228.title: Pascal's Hell
oa:W7215115228.abstract: ABSTRACT Expected utility maximization with unbounded utilities implies that tiny probabilities of huge positive or negative payoffs can dominate overall expected‐utility calculations. In other words, it leads to fanaticism . Fanaticism is counterintuitive, as illustrated by cases such as Pascal's Mugging and the St. Petersburg paradox. However, these cases do not illustrate the most counterintuitive implications of fanaticism. This paper shows, in the form of a dialogue, how a world filled with fanatical agents can be almost certain to be devoid of value—and by their own choice. The case presented here does not involve infinities, and it avoids the criticisms that have been raised against earlier cases.

oa:W7215174811.title: การวพากษแนวคดของบรอนวน ฟนนแกน ในบทความ "การเสยงโชคของพระพทธเจาและการเดมพนของปสกาล"
oa:W7215174811.abstract: The objective of this research article is to critique Bronwyn Finnigan's ideas in 'The Buddha's Lucky Throw and Pascal's Wager' by primarily studying related documents. The research method used is philosophical argumentation. Finnigan proposes six key ideas: (1) The Buddha and Pascal used the same type of reasoning in their respective wagers, including dominance reasoning. The researchers agree. (2) The Buddha's wager does not mention infinite value. The researchers disagree, citing the Apannaka Sutta, which mentions Nirvana—a concept that could be considered infinite value in Buddhism. (3) There is no evidence of karma and rebirth. However, the researchers disagrees, arguing that case studies of individuals who report past-life memories may constitute such evidence, and that, in some instances, truth and evidence need not necessarily coincide. (4) The wager in the Apannaka Sutta conflicts with the Kalama Sutta because there is no proof of the truth until one can know it for oneself through meditation. The researchers disagree because, in some cases, self-knowledge can be gained through thought. (5) The doctrine of anattā is often regarded as incompatible with the concept of rebirth. However, the researchers disagree, arguing that the process of death and rebirth of the five aggregates can be coherently explained through the principles of the three characteristics, the law of dhamma continuity, and dependent origination. (6) The wager presented in the Apannaka Sutta appears unconvincing when it assumes that those who accept the doctrines of karma and rebirth will consequently behave morally. The researchers disagree with this assumption and counters it by referencing empirical studies on belief in heaven and hell, as well as research on the effectiveness of graphic warn

oa:W7215277249.title: Leibniz's Theodicy "the Best Possible World" in the Context of Insurgency, Kidnapping and Banditry in Nigeria
oa:W7215277249.abstract: The problem of evil is a major philosophical issue that faces all humans irrespective of their religious persuasions and nationalities. In recent times some tragic happenings in Nigeria such as insurgency, kidnapping, banditry, and armed robbery has befallen the nation which are perceived as evil. This paper sets out to answer the question of why a good God will permit such evil in Nigeria. Leibniz’s theodicy of the “The best possible world” is analysed and contextualized as a template of perceived solution. Therefore, the methods adopted in this paper are contextual and phenomenological analysis. The findings show that Leibniz’s theodicy of “the best possible world” is logically applicable to Nigeria; God optimizes a world between simplicity, harmony, and productivity and has given human beings a world that is the best for them among many other possible worlds. Evil and Good are products of God’s sovereignty. The paper concludes and suggests that the evil and the good of Nigeria make the nation the best of all possible nations for Nigerians. A thorough philosophizing is recommended as a way forward. Nigerians should therefore adopt a philosophical attitude in the face of challenges (evil) confronting the nation.

oa:W7215329388.title: LIBERTATEA PERSONALĂ ȘI ARGUMENTELE PRUDENŢIALE SAU PRAGMATICE
authors: Ps. lect. univ. dr. Virgiliu Peicu
oa:W7215329388.venue: Journal for Freedom of Conscience (Jurnalul Libertății de Conștiință)
oa:W7215329388.abstract: Personal Freedom and Prudential or Pragmatic Arguments The study introduces a category of arguments about God’s existence and the belief in Him which is different from the ontological, cosmological and teleological arguments. Called prudential or pragmatic arguments, they may provide powerful reasons for personal faith and freedom. The most wellknown pragmatic arguments were developed by Blaise Pascal (1623-1662) and William James (1842-1910). The arguments developed by Blaise Pascal and William James are prudential or pragmatic because they seek to make a rational decision (primarily praxis, prudence) about the existence or non-existence of God. When they are internalized and believed, they lead to personal freedom (of conscience).

oa:W7215976613.title: Nothing in God
oa:W7215976613.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7215976613.abstract: Classical monotheism describes God as infinite, all-having, and necessarily existent. This paper asks whether these three descriptions can be held together when “all-having” is read strictly, so that it covers not only everything that is but also non-being. I defend a conditional thesis: if divine infinity requires strict inclusion of non-being itself (and not merely of a representation of it), then strict all-inclusiveness, necessary existence, and classical logic cannot all be true of God. The thesis yields a dilemma for theism: either divine all-inclusiveness must be restricted (for instance, to being and to perfections), or God must be placed beyond the constraints of logic. I offer three routes toward the key premise (a completeness argument, a comparison between two conceptions of God, and an argument from specific privations), examine the main objections, and relate the argument to Tillich’s treatment of non-being in God, Cantor’s Absolute Infinite, dialetheic theology, and Aquinas’s objection from contraries. I do not claim to refute theism. The result is a constraint on how the divine attributes may be defined together. Keywords: divine infinity; non-being; necessary existence; omni-inclusiveness; dialetheism; philosophy of religion

oa:W7216211021.title: The Existence of God: A New Way
oa:W7216211021.abstract: Abstract This article addresses the ‘discrepancy issue’ in contemporary analytic philosophy of religion, whereby Richard Swinburne’s probabilistic approach and Graham Oppy’s worldview analysis reach opposing conclusions from substantially the same evidence. In response, it sketches a new abductive argument for God’s existence by developing Peter Lipton’s notion of Inference to the Best Explanation into the method of ‘Virtue-IBE’, which compares rival theories by scoring their theoretical virtues. Virtue-IBE is offered as an improvement upon existing approaches and is applied to Bare Theism, as developed by Swinburne, Worldview Naturalism, as defended by Oppy, and Trope-Theoretic Theism, as proposed in this work (and earlier work), across six broad features of the physical world. On this assessment, Trope-Theoretic Theism, which identifies God as a maximal power trope, emerges as the loveliest, and therefore the best, of the three theories considered. The resulting conjunction of method and theory ultimately provides the basis for a new abductive case for God’s existence.

oa:W7217040306.title: La predestinazione in San Paolo
oa:W7217040306.venue: Lexicon Philosophicum: International Journal for the History of Texts and Ideas
oa:W7217040306.abstract: The idea of predestination, although the word is not used in Biblical Hebrew, is rooted in Old Testament episodes in which God is said to ‘choose’ or to ‘call’ specific human beings He knew in advance (before they were born) for prophetic missions. The leading concepts are therefore the Creator’s foreknowledge and absolute sovereignty, so that the unfolding of all events on earth cannot but fulfil his eternally outlined plan. This idea is emphasized in the Dead Sea Scrolls. In a similar way, Paul (Rom 8, 29), employing the Greek verb for ‘predefine’, explains the link between divine Foreknowledge and Predestination of those who are saved. Yet the predestinarian doctrine inevitably conflicts with the equally important requirement of free will and moral responsibility, performing the precepts of the Covenant; so, the prevailing tendency of pharisaic-rabbinical Judaism, and also of the Christian Church, has been an ambivalent coexistence of both God’s predestination and human freedom of choice. Gnosticism also embodies the ambivalence. In any case, the Gnostic predestination is very different from the Biblical one: it is not a divine absolute decision regarding single individuals, but the logical outcome of the kind of ‘nature’ to which they belong. English title: The Beginnings of the Idea of Predestination

oa:W84542211.title: Cosmological Argument: A Pragmatic Defense
oa:W84542211.venue: European Journal for Philosophy of Religion
oa:W84542211.abstract: We formulate a sort of “generic” Cosmological argument, i.e., a Cosmological argument that shares premises (e.g., “contingent, concretely existing entities have a cause”) with numerous versions of the argument. We then defend each of the premises by offering pragmatic arguments for them. We show that an endorsement of each premise will lead to an increase in expected utility; so in the absence of strong evidence that the premises are false, it is rational to endorse them. Therefore, it is rational to endorse the Cosmological argument, and so rational to endorse theism. We then consider possible objections.

oa:W856494257.title: The impossibility of an a priori resolution to newcomb's problem
oa:W856494257.abstract: Newcomb's Problem supposes that there are two boxes, an opaque and a transparent box. The transparent box contains $1,000. The opaque box contains either $1,000,000 or it contains nothing. You can take both boxes or take only the opaque box. The opaque \nbox's contents are determined by an extremely accurate predictor. If the predictor thinks \nyou will take only the opaque box, it places $1,000,000 in the opaque box. If the predictor thinks you will take both boxes, it places nothing in the opaque box. Arguments for taking both boxes have advocated ignoring the predictor's efficacy in decision-making. Causal decision theory developed and formalized this approach to decision-making. Its foremost competitor is evidential decision theory. In its simplest interpretation, evidential decision theory recommends taking just the opaque box. Causal decision theory, as well as attempts to rework evidential decision theory, lead to ambiguous prescriptions. These decision theories produce different prescriptions given different commitments about free will. We should prefer avoiding decision theories that lead to ambiguities whenever there is a decision theory that does not produce ambiguities. We have just such a decision theory: Jeffrey's original formulation of evidential decision theory does not require one to accept a particular position on free will to generate unambiguous prescriptions. Jeffrey's original formulation of evidential decision theory therefore should be preferred over causal decision theory.

oa:W998391039.title: Religious belief without evidence
oa:W998391039.abstract: We began this book by considering the evidentialist objection to religious belief. The objection, as you will recall, insists that all beliefs – with religious beliefs as no exception – must enjoy the support of adequate evidence if we are to believe them rationally. Most evidentialists insist that one not only have evidence, but also that one see how and to what degree one's evidence supports the target belief. In the light of this requirement, it is quite plain how the evidentialist's demand is congruent with the natural theologian's practice of forming arguments for God's existence, whose premises and strength of conclusion are evident. In this chapter, we consider two positions that, for differing reasons, do not attempt to meet the evidentialist demand, but reject it. Pascal is famous for thinking that, even if theism cannot be underwritten by so-called proofs for God's existence, belief in God is nevertheless rational on prudential grounds, because of the good ends religious belief brings about. Second, we shall explore a position most famously forwarded by Alvin Plantinga, referred to frequently as “Reformed epistemology”, stemming from the fact that he, and fellow Reformed epistemologists follow John Calvin and Martin Luther's rejection of natural theology. Belief in God, they argue, should be accepted as “properly basic”, without the need for argumentative support. Pragmatic arguments Pascal, to whom the reader has already been introduced, was no stranger to the tradition of natural theology.
